name: Chebyshev's Inequality
statement: For any random variable with finite variance, the probability it deviates from its mean by k standard deviations or more is at most 1/k².
meaning: This inequality gives a universal, distribution-free bound on how much probability mass can lie far from the mean, using only the mean and variance. It guarantees that extreme deviations are rare in a precise, quantifiable sense even when the exact shape of the distribution is unknown. For k=2 it guarantees at least 75% of the probability mass lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
mechanism: The inequality follows from applying Markov’s inequality to the non-negative random variable (X−μ)², since the probability of deviating by k standard deviations equals the probability that (X−μ)² is at least k²σ². Because it makes no assumption about the shape of the distribution, the bound is generally very loose compared with distribution-specific bounds such as the far tighter exponential tails of a normal distribution.

examples.text: If articles in a journal average 1,000 words with a standard deviation of 200 words, the inequality guarantees at least 75% of articles have between 600 and 1,400 words (k=2, bound 1/4).
Chebyshev used the inequality to prove his version of the weak law of large numbers, showing sample averages converge in probability to the true mean as sample size grows.
Because it requires only a finite variance, the inequality applies identically to any distribution — discrete or continuous, symmetric or skewed — unlike bounds that assume normality.

whyItMatters: It is one of the few tail bounds requiring no assumption about the underlying distribution beyond a finite variance, making it foundational for proving convergence results such as the weak law of large numbers, and it underlies many concentration-of-measure arguments throughout probability and statistics.
limits: The bound is often very loose for well-behaved distributions like the normal, where actual tail probabilities are far smaller than 1/k² suggests. For k≤1 the inequality is trivial, since 1/k²≥1 exceeds any valid probability, giving no information.
misreadings: It is often mistaken for an exact probability statement rather than a worst-case upper bound; many assume it gives a tight or typical estimate of tail probability rather than a guarantee valid for the worst possible distribution.
origin: First stated without a general proof by Irénée-Jules Bienaymé in 1853; Pafnuty Chebyshev, unaware of that work, published a general proof in 1867, which is why it is also called the Bienaymé–Chebyshev inequality. Chebyshev’s student Andrey Markov gave another proof in his 1884 thesis.

sources.text: Chebyshev’s inequality, Wikipedia. — the 1/k² bound and the Bienaymé (1853)/Chebyshev (1867) attribution history.
"Chebyshev’s inequality," Encyclopaedia Britannica. — that the probability of exceeding k standard deviations is at most 1/k², with shared Bienaymé credit.
